dropped.reason: Flawed question: the photon energy is $hc/\lambda=6.2$ eV, so the work function would be 2.2 eV, which matches none of the options (the school withdrew it and gave every student the mark)

questions.question: Rachel is driving her car at a constant speed around a curve of fixed radius. Which of the following correctly describes the acceleration of Rachel's car?
questions.answer: At constant speed on a circle of fixed radius the centripetal acceleration $a=\frac{v^2}{r}$ has a constant magnitude, but it always points towards the centre of the circle, so its direction changes continuously (B).
options: Magnitude: constant; direction: constant
Magnitude: constant; direction: changes
Magnitude: changes; direction: constant
Magnitude: changes; direction: changes

questions.question: While calibrating a spectrometer attached to a telescope, Yatha records a hydrogen line in the Balmer series with a wavelength of 656.28 nm. Later, a star is observed, and the same hydrogen line in its spectrum is recorded as 680 nm. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: 680 nm is longer than 656.28 nm, so the line is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum (red shift). A red shift means the source is moving away from the observer (C).
options: The star is blue shifted and moving towards us.
The star is red shifted and moving towards us.
The star is red shifted and moving away from us.
The star is blue shifted and is moving away from us.

questions.question: According to Max Planck, which characteristic of an object determined the peak wavelength of radiation emitted by a hot object?
questions.answer: In Planck's black-body model the spectrum and its peak wavelength depend only on the temperature (Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}T=b$), not on the material or shape (B).
options: The type of material the object is made of.
The temperature of the object.
The type of material and its temperature.
The temperature of the object and its shape.

questions.question: Ravindu is driving his father's SUV around a banked circular track at constant height. Which of the following correctly shows the forces acting on the SUV?
questions.answer: For an ideal banked track the only real forces are the weight $mg$ (down) and the normal reaction force from the track (perpendicular to the surface). The horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force and the vertical component balances $mg$ (constant height). $F_c$ is the net force, not an additional force, so it must not be drawn separately, and friction is not needed. Diagram A shows only these two forces (A).
options: ![Diagram A](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q4a.png)
![Diagram B](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q4b.png)
![Diagram C](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q4c.png)
![Diagram D](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q4d.png)

questions.question: The individual stars in a single star cluster are plotted on a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, as shown (spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M from left to right). The relative under-representation of O and B type stars is most likely due to:
questions.answer: The diagram shows a main-sequence turn-off with a red-giant branch, which is characteristic of an old cluster. Massive O and B stars burn their hydrogen very rapidly and have short main-sequence lifetimes, so they have already used up their core hydrogen and left the main sequence to become red giants (and later supernovae), leaving the upper main sequence under-populated (C).
options: the cluster being too young for these stars to have formed yet.
too much gas and dust existing between the stars preventing such stars from forming.
these stars having depleted their hydrogen fuel and becoming red giants.
the main sequence stars that formed in the cluster were not sufficiently large.

questions.question: What was Schrödinger's main contribution to the current model of the atom?
questions.answer: Schrödinger developed the wave equation for the electron, which gives the probability distribution of the electron around the nucleus (orbitals) and is a foundation of modern quantum mechanics (C). Diffraction experiments were by Davisson and Germer, and Bohr was the first to apply quantum ideas to the atom.
options: Diffraction experiments verifying the wave properties of electrons.
His work was the basis of the Bohr model of the atom.
His wave equations were very important in the development of modern quantum mechanics.
He was the first to apply quantum ideas to the understanding of the atom.

questions.question: A satellite is in a stable geostationary orbit around the Earth. Which of the options below best shows the satellite's path if the gravitational force on it was somehow removed when it was at point X?
questions.answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force. With no net force, by Newton's first law the satellite continues in a straight line at constant velocity, along the tangent to the orbit at X (A).
options: ![Option A](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q7a.png)
![Option B](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q7b.png)
![Option C](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q7c.png)
![Option D](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q7d.png)

questions.question: A reason that the observations from the Geiger–Marsden experiment were unexpected at the time was that:
questions.answer: Before the experiment the accepted model was Thomson's 'plum pudding' model, in which negative electrons are embedded throughout a diffuse positive sphere. This model predicted only small deflections of alpha particles, so the observed large-angle scattering and back-scattering was unexpected (D).
options: atoms were believed to have a positive nucleus.
atoms were thought to be capable of reflecting alpha particles.
electrons were believed to be orbiting the nucleus.
atoms were thought to have the negative charges embedded throughout a continuous positive fluid.

questions.question: Two masses have a gravitational force of 12 N between them. If the distance between them is doubled, what would be the new gravitational force between them?
questions.answer: $F\propto\frac1{r^2}$, so doubling $r$ reduces $F$ by a factor of 4: $\frac{12}{4}=3$ N (A).
options: 3 N
6 N

questions.question: How much work is done on an electron being accelerated between two charged plates with a voltage drop of 20 V?
The diagram shows a DC electric motor, but when a current flows through the coil, it does not turn. Which of the following is required so that the coil turns?
questions.answer: In the position shown the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field, so the forces on the two sides of the coil act along the same line (the coil's axis) and give zero torque ($\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ with $\theta=0$). The coil is stuck at this 'dead spot'. It must be started from a different position so the torque is non-zero; changing the size or direction of the current or the field strength will not produce a torque in this position (A).
options: The starting point of the coil must be changed.
The magnetic field must be reduced.
The magnitude of the current must be increased.
The direction of the current must be reversed.

questions.question: Stirling observed that a space probe at rest is 40 m long. However, when he sees the space probe travelling in space it is only 32 m long. What was the speed of the space probe relative to Stirling?
questions.answer: Length contraction: $L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$, so $\frac{32}{40}=0.80=\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$, giving $\frac{v^2}{c^2}=1-0.64=0.36$ and $v=0.60c$ (A).

questions.question: A Physics student got a flat tyre and had to undo the wheel nuts using a wheel wrench. Which of the following shows that they have the poorest understanding possible of how to undo the wheel nuts with a minimum applied force?
questions.answer: Torque is $\tau=r_\perp F=rF\sin\theta$. To minimise the force needed, the force should be applied perpendicular to the wrench ($\sin\theta=1$) and as far from the nut as possible (large $r$), as in D. The poorest understanding combines both mistakes: a small lever arm and an angle that is not $90^\circ$, giving the smallest torque for a given force. This is B.
options: The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the smallest distance possible from the wheel nut.
The force should be applied at $45^\circ$ to the wheel wrench at the smallest distance possible from the wheel nut.
The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the middle distance along the tyre lever.
The force should be applied at right angles to the wheel wrench at the largest distance from the wheel nut possible.

questions.question: Photons of wavelength $\lambda$ are incident on a metallic surface in a vacuum. The number of photons incident on the surface per second is $n$. No electrons are emitted from the surface. Which of the following actions is more likely to cause electrons to be emitted from the surface?
questions.answer: Emission requires each photon to have energy $hf\ge\phi$. No emission means $hf<\phi$. Increasing the number of photons (intensity) does not help, since each electron absorbs a single photon. Decreasing the wavelength increases the frequency and photon energy, which could exceed the work function (B). Changing to a different metal could help only if the new metal had a lower work function, which is not guaranteed.
options: Decrease the frequency of the incident light.
Decrease the wavelength, $\lambda$, of the incident light.
Increase the number of photons per second, $n$, incident on the surface.
Change to a different metallic surface.

questions.question: Maxwell's equations apply to the:
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations describe light as an electromagnetic wave, predicting its wave behaviour and speed. They do not explain the photoelectric effect, which requires a particle (photon) model (D).
options: particle model of light only.
particle and wave models of light.
explanation of the photoelectric effect.
wave model of light only.

questions.question: A charged particle $q$ enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ at velocity $v$ and follows a circular path of radius $r$. If the magnitude of the magnetic field was doubled and the other variables were kept constant, what would the new radius be?
questions.answer: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r=\frac{mv}{qB}\propto\frac1B$. Doubling $B$ halves the radius: $r/2$ (B).

questions.question: A conductor connected to an ammeter is moved by a force $F$ through a magnetic field (directed into the page) in the direction shown (to the right). The direction of the conventional current in the conductor and the reason why it must be in this direction is:
questions.answer: Using the right-hand palm rule for a positive charge moving right through a field into the page, the force (and so the conventional current) is up the page. This direction is required by Lenz's law (conservation of energy): the induced current's own magnetic force on the conductor must oppose the motion, so work done by the applied force $F$ is transferred to electrical energy (B).
options: Up the page; the motor effect
Up the page; the law of conservation of energy
Down the page; the law of conservation of energy
No current; there is not a complete circuit

questions.question: Michelson and Morley expected to see a change in the interference pattern in their experiment, yet they obtained a null result. Why did they obtain a null result?
questions.answer: The school's key gives A: the result was consistent with the principle of relativity (no experiment can detect absolute motion through a stationary aether, and the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames), whereas a positive result would have identified a preferred frame. The apparatus was sensitive enough (B is false), the null result was repeatable (C), and the experiment (1887) pre-dated Einstein's postulates (1905) (D).
options: A positive result would violate the principle of relativity.
The Earth's speed through space is too small compared to the speed of light for the experiment to give a significant result.
Any variation in the speed of light could be explained by experimental errors.
Einstein had proven that the speed of light was a constant in a particular medium.

questions.question: Danindu moves a square copper plate at a constant speed through a magnetic field (dots show a field out of the page), as shown. The plate is shown at positions P, Q, R and S. Which of the following best shows the emf induced in the plate?
questions.answer: An emf is induced only while the flux through the plate is changing ($\varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$). While the plate is entering the field the flux increases at a constant rate (constant emf of one sign); when it is fully inside a uniform field the flux is constant, so the emf is zero; as it leaves the flux decreases at a constant rate, giving a constant emf of the opposite sign; outside the field the emf is zero. Constant-valued sections (not ramps) because the speed is constant. This is graph B (the school's answer).
options: ![Graph A](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q20a.png)
![Graph B](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q20b.png)
![Graph C](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q20c.png)
![Graph D](assets/img/phys-2022-baulkham-hills/q20d.png)

questions.question: Mars has a mass of $6.39\times10^{23}$ kg and a diameter of $6.679\times10^{6}$ m, and a negligible atmosphere. Calculate the acceleration due to gravity that astronauts would experience on the surface of Mars.

On Mars (surface gravity $3.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, radius $3.3395\times10^6$ m, negligible atmosphere) a 1.25 kg food canister is thrown upward at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial velocity of $2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the maximum distance the canister rises above the launch point (and state its maximum distance from the centre of Mars).
questions.answer: Vertically, $u_y=2.5\sin25^\circ=1.0565\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v_y=0$ at the top. Taking up as positive with $a=-3.8218\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: $v_y^2=u_y^2+2as$ gives $s=\frac{-u_y^2}{2a}=\frac{-(1.0565)^2}{2(-3.8218)}=0.146$ m. So the canister rises 0.146 m above the launch point, i.e. its maximum distance from the centre of Mars is the radius of Mars (plus the launch height) plus 0.146 m, about $3.34\times10^6$ m. (The school's key gives 0.146 m.)

questions.question: On Mars (surface gravity $3.82\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, negligible atmosphere) a food canister is thrown at an angle of $25^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial velocity of $2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a height of 2 m above level ground. How far does the canister land from where it was thrown (horizontal distance)?

Calculate the minimum velocity that astronauts would need to throw a food canister vertically from the surface of Mars (mass $6.39\times10^{23}$ kg, radius $3.3395\times10^6$ m) if it was to just escape Mars' gravitational field.
questions.answer: For escape, the initial kinetic energy equals the energy needed to reach infinity: $\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.39\times10^{23}}{3.3395\times10^6}}=5.05\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (about 5052 m s$^{-1}$).

questions.question: In 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) was placed in orbit around the Earth. In the diagram (not to scale), Earth and HST are drawn on orbits around the Sun with identical orbital periods. This appears to contradict Kepler's law of periods. Fully explain why it is possible for the HST to orbit the Sun with the same orbital period as the Earth.
questions.answer: Kepler's law of periods, $\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, relates the period of a body to its orbital radius for bodies orbiting the **same central mass** $M$. The Earth orbits the Sun, so $M$ is the mass of the Sun, whereas the HST orbits the Earth, so $M$ is the mass of the Earth. The diagram is misleading because the HST is not in a separate orbit around the Sun: it orbits the Earth, and the Earth carries it around the Sun, so the HST's period around the Sun is the Earth's period (one year). The Sun's gravitational force on the HST is much weaker than the Earth's at the HST's altitude, so the HST stays bound to Earth and follows it. There is therefore no contradiction with Kepler's law, which applies separately to the HST–Earth and Earth–Sun systems.

questions.question: Protons are accelerated in the Large Hadron Collider to travel at $2.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The LHC has a diameter of $8\times10^{3}$ m. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of these protons.

Protons in the Large Hadron Collider (diameter $8\times10^{3}$ m) travel at $2.2\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ around a circular path. Calculate the momentum of a proton at that speed and the force required to keep it on the circular path.
questions.answer: At $2.2\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ($v/c=0.0073$) the Lorentz factor is $\gamma\approx1.00003$, so relativistic effects are negligible and $p=mv=1.673\times10^{-27}\times2.2\times10^{6}=3.7\times10^{-21}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. The path has radius $r=4\times10^3$ m, so the centripetal force is $F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{1.673\times10^{-27}\times(2.2\times10^{6})^2}{4\times10^{3}}=2.0\times10^{-18}$ N. (The school's key gives $2.2\times10^{-18}$ N; recalculating gives $2.0\times10^{-18}$ N.)

questions.question: Assess the validity of the following statement: 'Particle accelerators cannot accelerate particles to any speed beyond the speed of light.'
questions.answer: The statement is valid. According to special relativity the relativistic momentum $p=\gamma m_0v$ and total energy $E=\gamma m_0c^2$ both increase without limit as $v\to c$ because $\gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\to\infty$. Accelerating a particle with mass to $v=c$ would require an infinite amount of energy (and force), which cannot be supplied, so particles can be accelerated ever closer to $c$ but can never reach it, let alone exceed it. This is confirmed in accelerators such as the LHC, where particles gain energy and momentum but their speed only approaches $c$.

questions.question: Two parallel plates are 2.50 mm apart and connected to a power supply which produces a potential difference of 320 V. An electron is at rest at point P between the plates. Calculate the force acting on the electron.
questions.answer: $E=\frac Vd=\frac{320}{2.50\times10^{-3}}=1.28\times10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$ and $F=qE=1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.28\times10^{5}=2.05\times10^{-14}$ N, directed towards the positive plate.

questions.question: Two parallel plates are 2.50 mm apart and connected to a 320 V supply. An electron is at rest at point P between the plates and experiences a force of $2.05\times10^{-14}$ N. Describe quantitatively the effect of the field on the electron's motion.
questions.answer: The force on the electron is directed towards the positive plate (opposite to the field direction, since the electron is negative). From $F=ma$, $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{2.05\times10^{-14}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=2.25\times10^{16}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. So the electron accelerates uniformly from rest towards the positive plate at $2.25\times10^{16}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. (The school's key prints this as $10^{-16}$, a typo.)

questions.question: Describe ONE experiment conducted by a scientist that provided a previously unknown property of the electron.
questions.answer: **Millikan's oil-drop experiment** showed that electric charge is quantised. Oil droplets were sprayed from a nozzle into the space between two charged parallel plates; they became charged by friction with the air as they were sprayed. Millikan adjusted the voltage (electric field $E$) between the plates until a droplet was suspended at rest, so that the upward electric force equalled the downward weight: $qE=mg$, giving $q=\frac{mg}{E}$. He found that the charge on every droplet was an integer multiple of a smallest value, about $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C. This showed that the charge of the electron is a fundamental unit of charge: charge exists only in whole multiples of the electron's charge.

questions.question: A phone charger is plugged into a 240 V AC supply. The transformer in the charger converts this to an output of 6 V DC. The phone draws a 1 A current from the charger when being charged. Determine the current drawn by the charger on the 240 V supply.
questions.answer: For an ideal transformer, $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$, so $I_p=\frac{V_sI_s}{V_p}=\frac{6\times1}{240}=0.025$ A $=2.5\times10^{-2}$ A.

questions.question: Use a labelled diagram to model the structure of the transformer in a phone charger (240 V AC input, 6 V output).
questions.answer: The diagram should show: a closed, laminated soft-iron core (a rectangular loop); a **primary coil** (connected to the 240 V AC supply) wound on one side of the core and a **secondary coil** (connected to the output/load) wound on the other side, each insulated from the core and from one another. Since the output is much lower than the input, the primary coil has many more turns than the secondary coil ($n_p>n_s$): a step-down transformer, with $\frac{V_p}{V_s}=\frac{n_p}{n_s}=\frac{240}{6}=40$. Label the AC supply, primary coil, secondary coil, load and laminated iron core.

questions.question: Explain TWO methods that could maximise the efficiency of a phone charger's transformer.
questions.answer: **1. Laminated core:** build the core from thin sheets of iron separated by insulating material, with the layers parallel to the direction of the magnetic flux. This reduces the size of the eddy currents induced in the core, so less energy is lost as heat, which increases efficiency. **2. Better linkage of flux (soft-iron core and coil winding):** use a soft iron core and wind the primary and secondary coils close together (or over each other with insulation between), so that nearly all the flux produced by the primary passes through the secondary. Reducing flux leakage means more of the input energy is transferred to the secondary coil. (Alternative: use thicker, low-resistance copper wire to reduce resistive $I^2R$ heating in the coils.)

questions.question: A handle of length $L$ is used to rotate a cylinder containing multiple copper windings between two permanent magnets (a simple generator). When the cylinder is rotated, an emf is generated across the copper windings. Describe and explain quantitatively how doubling the handle length ($L$) will change the emf generated in the copper windings in the cylinder if the handle continues to be turned at the same angular velocity.
questions.answer: The emf is given by Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, where the flux through the coil is $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ and $\theta=\omega t$. So $\varepsilon_{\max}=NBA\omega$, which depends on the number of turns, the field strength, the coil area and the angular velocity, but not on the length of the handle. The handle and cylinder rotate together, so at the same angular velocity the coil cuts the field lines at the same rate and the emf is **unchanged** (it does not double). A longer handle increases the torque produced by a given applied force (the lever arm, $\tau=r_\perp F$, doubles), so the same turning torque is obtained for half the applied force, but the emf stays the same.

questions.question: Clearly explain the production of absorption spectra by the atmosphere of stars.
questions.answer: The hot, dense photosphere of a star emits a continuous (black-body) spectrum. This light passes through the cooler, less dense gases of the star's outer atmosphere. Atoms in the atmosphere absorb photons whose energy exactly matches the difference between two of their energy levels ($E=hf=E_2-E_1$), raising electrons to higher levels. The atoms then de-excite by re-emitting photons of the same frequency, but in random directions, so far fewer photons of those frequencies continue in the original direction towards the observer. The observed spectrum therefore shows a continuous background crossed by dark absorption lines at the wavelengths characteristic of the elements in the star's atmosphere.

questions.question: Describe clearly how the study of a star's spectrum can give us information about TWO specific features of that star.
questions.answer: **Chemical composition:** the pattern of dark absorption lines in the star's spectrum is unique to each element, so comparing the wavelengths of the lines with known laboratory spectra of elements (e.g. hydrogen's Balmer series) identifies the elements present in the star's atmosphere. **Radial (translational) velocity:** the absorption lines are shifted relative to their laboratory wavelengths by the Doppler effect. A shift to longer wavelengths (red shift) shows the star is moving away from us and a shift to shorter wavelengths (blue shift) shows it is moving towards us; the speed is found from $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=\frac vc$. (Other acceptable features: surface temperature from the peak of the black-body curve using Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}T=b$; rotational velocity from line broadening; gas pressure from line widths.)

questions.question: Outline Hubble's observations and their significance in terms of our understanding of the nature of the universe.
questions.answer: Hubble measured the red shift of the absorption lines in the spectra of other galaxies and found that nearly all galaxies are red-shifted, i.e. moving away from us. He also found that the recession velocity is proportional to the galaxy's distance ($v=H_0d$), so more distant galaxies recede faster. This showed that the universe is expanding, which led to the hypothesis of the Big Bang (everything was once concentrated in a much smaller volume). He also showed that some 'nebulae' were actually separate galaxies far outside the Milky Way, which showed that the universe is far larger than the Milky Way alone.

questions.question: For electricity to be transmitted over large distances between generators and households, transformers are used. Two transmissions take place over the same transmission lines at different times: Transmission A: 28 kV AC; Transmission B: 280 kV AC (the same power is supplied at the start of each). Compare the power losses that occur in transmissions A and B. Include relevant equations and calculations in your response.
questions.answer: The power supplied is $P=VI$, so for the same power the line current is $I=\frac PV$. The power lost in the line (resistance $R$) is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R=\left(\frac PV\right)^2R\propto\frac1{V^2}$. Transmission B has a voltage 10 times larger, so its current is 10 times smaller and its loss is $10^2=100$ times smaller: $\frac{P_{\text{loss,A}}}{P_{\text{loss,B}}}=\left(\frac{280}{28}\right)^2=100$. Transmission A loses 100 times as much power in the lines as transmission B.

questions.question: With the aid of a labelled diagram, outline Bohr's model of the atom and state the limitations of the model.
questions.answer: **Bohr's model (diagram: a small central positive nucleus with electrons in circular orbits labelled $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, and an arrow showing a transition with a photon emitted):** electrons orbit the nucleus only in certain allowed orbits (stationary states) with fixed, discrete energies. Electrons in these orbits do not radiate energy. Electrons can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference between the levels, $\Delta E=E_2-E_1=hf$. **Limitations:** it works well only for hydrogen and hydrogen-like (single electron) atoms and cannot explain the spectra of atoms with more electrons; it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines, the splitting of lines in magnetic fields (Zeeman effect) or fine structure; it gives no reason why orbits are stable (an accelerating charge should radiate according to Maxwell); and it treats the electron as a particle in a definite orbit, which conflicts with the wave nature of the electron and the uncertainty principle (later replaced by Schrödinger's quantum mechanical model).

questions.question: Outline experimental evidence that supported ONE of Bohr's postulates and explain how the experimental evidence provided this support.
questions.answer: **Postulate:** electrons can only exist in orbits with discrete energy levels, and they emit or absorb a photon of energy $\Delta E=hf$ when moving between them. **Evidence:** the line emission spectrum of hydrogen. A discharge tube of hydrogen gas viewed through a spectroscope shows only a few discrete bright lines (the Balmer series: 656.3, 486.1, 434.0, 410.2 nm, ...), not a continuous spectrum. This supports the postulate because if electrons could have any energy a continuous spectrum would be seen; discrete lines show only specific energy differences are allowed. Bohr's model predicts these wavelengths using $\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{n_f^2}-\frac1{n_i^2}\right)$, in agreement with the measured wavelengths.

questions.question: Fully explain the production of torque in the device shown (a simple DC motor: a rectangular coil between the poles of a magnet, with a split-ring commutator and graphite brushes). In your answer, refer to the diagram and include two relevant graphs.
questions.answer: The device is a simple DC motor. When current flows through the coil, each of the two sides of the coil that are perpendicular to the field experiences a force $F=nIlB\sin\theta$ (the motor effect), given by the right-hand palm rule. Because the current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, the forces are equal and opposite, so one side is pushed up and the other down, producing a torque about the axis, $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ ($\theta$ is the angle between the coil's plane normal and the field). The graphite brushes press against the split-ring commutator, which reverses the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical (zero torque) position. This ensures that the torque always acts in the same rotational sense, so the coil continues to rotate in one direction. **Graphs (see image):** (1) without a commutator the torque varies as $\sin\theta$ and reverses direction every half turn, so the coil would just oscillate; (2) with a split-ring commutator the torque is always in the same direction, varying between zero (coil plane perpendicular to the field) and a maximum (coil plane parallel to the field), $\tau\propto|\sin\theta|$.

questions.question: In 1911 Ejnar Hertzsprung and in 1913 Henry Norris Russell independently plotted the luminosity of stars versus their surface temperatures, as shown in the diagram. Identify the predominant nuclear reactions involved in the three groups A, B and C.
questions.answer: **Group A (upper right: giants):** helium fusion by the triple-alpha process (and CNO-cycle hydrogen fusion in a shell around the core). **Group B (lower left: white dwarfs):** no fusion occurs; they are cooling remnants. **Group C (lower main sequence, cool red dwarfs):** the proton–proton chain (hydrogen fusion), not the CNO cycle, since the core temperatures are lower.

questions.question: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram of luminosity against surface temperature, with reference to the diagram, outline the stellar evolution of the Sun.
questions.answer: The Sun is currently a main-sequence star (like those in the band running from top-left to bottom-right, near group C but hotter), fusing hydrogen into helium in its core by the proton–proton chain. When the core hydrogen is exhausted the core contracts and heats up, hydrogen fuses in a shell around it, and the outer layers expand and cool: the Sun moves off the main sequence to become a red giant (up and to the right, group A on the diagram), later fusing helium in its core. Finally, since the Sun is not massive enough to fuse heavier elements, the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the remaining core becomes a white dwarf (down and to the left, group B), which slowly cools.

questions.question: What evidence supports the classical wave model of light and what predictions can be made using this model? In your answer, include a relevant diagram and state TWO observations concerning light that are unable to be explained by the classical model.
questions.answer: **Evidence for the classical wave model.** In the 17th century Newton's particle (corpuscular) model competed with Huygens' wave model. The wave model was accepted because of experiments which only waves can explain: Young's double-slit experiment (1801) produced an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes, as the waves from the two slits interfered constructively and destructively; light also shows diffraction around obstacles and through single slits; polarisation (e.g. Malus's law) shows light is a transverse wave; and Foucault's measurement of the speed of light in water showed it to be slower than in air, as the wave model predicts (the particle model predicted faster). Maxwell's theory of electromagnetic waves gave the wave model a full theoretical basis. **Diagram:** a double-slit set-up (see image): monochromatic light incident on two slits, producing bright and dark fringes on a screen. **Predictions:** double-slit fringe spacing $\Delta y=\frac{\lambda L}{d}$ and $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ for gratings and slits; the intensity transmitted through polarisers, $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$; refraction ($n=\frac{c}{v}$) and the speed of light in a medium; and the speed of EM waves, $c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$. **Two observations the classical model cannot explain:** (1) *Black-body radiation* – the classical wave model predicts that intensity rises without limit at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe), but experiment shows a peak that depends on temperature; Planck explained it by quantised energy $E=hf$. (2) *The photoelectric effect* – electron emission depends on the frequency (not the intensity) of the light, has a threshold frequency, and is instantaneous, which the wave model cannot explain; Einstein explained it with photons, $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$.
